questions.question: What is the summary comparison of Java List, Set, and Map implementations?
questions.title: Collections Comparison
questions.direct_answer: **List** keeps order and allows duplicates (`ArrayList` for access, `LinkedList` for end-ops). **Set** stores unique elements (`HashSet` unordered, `LinkedHashSet` insertion order, `TreeSet` sorted). **Map** stores key-value pairs (`HashMap` unordered, `LinkedHashMap` ordered, `TreeMap` sorted by key). Choose by three axes: **duplicates vs unique**, **ordering**, and **access pattern**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can recall the whole landscape and the time complexity of each implementation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing up which structures are ordered vs sorted, or quoting wrong complexities
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Group implementations by Hash (O(1), unordered), Linked (ordered), Tree (sorted, O(log n)) — one mental model across Set and Map

sections.title: The Whole Landscape in One View
sections.content:
A **collection** is an object that holds a group of other values. Java sorts its collections into three families — **`List`**, **`Set`**, and **`Map`** — and almost every interview question starts with picking the right one.

**`List`** is an ordered sequence that **allows duplicates** and supports index access. **`Set`** **rejects duplicates**. **`Map`** stores **key-value pairs**, mapping each unique key to a value.

Within `Set` and `Map` there is one pattern worth memorising. The **`Hash`** variant is unordered and runs in O(1). The **`Linked`** variant preserves **insertion order**. The **`Tree`** variant keeps elements **sorted** at O(log n).

That single **Hash/Linked/Tree** idea carries across both. Once you know `HashSet` vs `LinkedHashSet` vs `TreeSet`, you already understand `HashMap` vs `LinkedHashMap` vs `TreeMap`.

> **Rule of thumb:** choose along three axes — duplicates vs unique, ordering, and access pattern.

sections.title: List / Set / Map Implementations
sections.content:
| Type | Implementation | Order | Duplicates | get/put/contains | Notable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| List | ArrayList | insertion | yes | O(1) get | default list |
| List | LinkedList | insertion | yes | O(n) get, O(1) ends | also a Deque |
| Set | HashSet | none | no | O(1) | fastest set |
| Set | LinkedHashSet | insertion | no | O(1) | order preserved |
| Set | TreeSet | sorted | no | O(log n) | NavigableSet |
| Map | HashMap | none | keys unique | O(1) | default map |
| Map | LinkedHashMap | insertion/access | keys unique | O(1) | LRU caches |
| Map | TreeMap | sorted by key | keys unique | O(log n) | range queries |

emerald|Set|~Unique elements|HashSet: O(1)|LinkedHashSet: order|TreeSet: sorted O(log n)

The whole landscape fits on one page once you draw it as a tree. ```mermaid flowchart TD P["Collections"] --> L["List
ordered, duplicates"] P --> S["Set
unique elements"] P --> M["Map
key to value"] S --> SH["HashSet
unordered, O(1)"] S --> SL["LinkedHashSet
insertion order"] S --> ST["TreeSet
sorted, O(log n)"] M --> MH["HashMap

insertion order"] M --> MT["TreeMap
sorted, O(log n)"] ``` The Hash, Linked, and Tree row under Set repeats exactly under Map — learn one and you get the other free.

sections.title: Wrong pick: a List when you need uniqueness
Right pick: the structure that matches the requirement
When to Use Each
sections.content:
Use a **List** when order matters and duplicates are allowed (a feed, a log, a cart). Use a **Set** when elements must be unique (visitor IDs, tags). Use a **Map** when you look things up by a key (id to object, word to count).

Then pick the variant: **Hash** for raw speed when order is irrelevant, **Linked** when you must preserve insertion order, **Tree** when you need sorted iteration or range queries.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing ordered with sorted.** `LinkedHashSet`/`LinkedHashMap` keep *insertion* order; `TreeSet`/`TreeMap` keep *sorted* order — these are not the same thing.
- **Using a `List` with `contains` for uniqueness.** That is an O(n) scan on every check; a `Set` gives O(1) membership and rejects duplicates for free.
- **Quoting wrong complexities.** `ArrayList.get` is O(1) but `LinkedList.get(i)` is O(n); `HashMap` is O(1) average while `TreeMap` is O(log n).
- **Defaulting to `TreeMap`/`TreeSet` when order does not matter.** You pay O(log n) for sorting you never use — reach for the Hash variants first.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **List** = ordered + duplicates; **Set** = unique; **Map** = key to value.
- One model across Set/Map: **Hash** (O(1), unordered), **Linked** (insertion order), **Tree** (sorted, O(log n)).
- `ArrayList` = default list; `LinkedList` = also a Deque.
- `HashMap`/`HashSet` are the defaults; switch for ordering or sorting needs.
- `TreeSet`/`TreeMap` give sorted order and range queries at O(log n).
- `LinkedHashMap` backs LRU caches via access order.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: There are three families of collections. List is an ordered sequence that allows duplicates and lets you access by index — ArrayList is the default, and LinkedList also acts as a deque. Set stores unique elements, no duplicates. Map maps unique keys to values. The trick that ties everything together is a single pattern that repeats inside both Set and Map. The Hash variant — HashSet and HashMap — is unordered and operates in constant time, so it's the fastest and the default. The Linked variant — LinkedHashSet and LinkedHashMap — preserves insertion order, and LinkedHashMap can also use access order, which is what you use to build an LRU cache. The Tree variant — TreeSet and TreeMap — keeps everything sorted, with log-n operations, and it supports range queries like headMap and tailMap. So once you understand HashSet versus LinkedHashSet versus TreeSet, you automatically understand the three maps too. To choose, I ask three questions. First, do I allow duplicates? If yes, List; if no, Set. Do I look things up by a key? Then Map. Second, does order matter? If insertion order matters, use a Linked variant; if I need sorting, use a Tree variant; otherwise use Hash for speed. Third, what's my access pattern — random access points to ArrayList, end-heavy points to a deque. That three-question framework, plus the Hash-Linked-Tree pattern, lets me place any collection quickly and quote the right complexity for each.

questions.question: How do you choose the right Java collection for a given problem?
questions.title: Choosing the Right Collection
questions.direct_answer: Ask a short decision sequence: do you need **key-value lookup** (Map) or just elements? Must elements be **unique** (Set) or are **duplicates allowed** (List)? Then pick the variant by **ordering** (Hash = none, Linked = insertion, Tree = sorted) and **access pattern** (`ArrayList` for random access, `ArrayDeque` for queues).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you have a repeatable decision process rather than memorized defaults
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Jumping straight to ArrayList/HashMap without asking about uniqueness, ordering, or lookup
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Phrase it as a decision tree and mention thread-safety (ConcurrentHashMap) as a final branch

sections.title: A Repeatable Decision Process
sections.content:
Every program needs to store data somewhere, and Java gives you many containers to choose from. Picking the right one comes down to a short series of yes/no questions, not memorising defaults.

Start with the **shape of the data**: are you looking things up by a **key**? If so, you need a `Map`. If not, are **duplicates** allowed? Duplicates with order means `List`; uniqueness means `Set`.

Once the family is fixed, pick the **variant** by ordering — no order, insertion order, or sorted — and by **access pattern**, like random index versus end operations.

A final branch is **thread safety**. Under concurrency, reach for `ConcurrentHashMap` or `CopyOnWriteArrayList` instead of the plain versions.

> **Default rule:** when nothing special applies, `ArrayList` and `HashMap` are the right starting point.

sections.title: Collection Decision Tree
Step 1: Key Lookup vs Elements
sections.content: If your access is 'given this id, get that object', you need a **Map**. Map turns lookups into O(1) instead of an O(n) scan through a list. If you only ever hold and iterate elements, move on to the next question.

sections.title: Step 2: Duplicates vs Unique, then Ordering
sections.content: For element storage: duplicates allowed and ordered means **List** (`ArrayList` default; `ArrayDeque` if it's really a queue/stack). Uniqueness means **Set**. Then choose ordering: **Hash** for speed and no order, **Linked** to preserve insertion order, **Tree** for sorted iteration or range queries. Finally, if multiple threads access it, switch to the concurrent variant.

sections.title: The Decision in Code
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reaching for `ArrayList` on reflex.** Always ask about lookup, uniqueness, and ordering first — the right structure often is not a list at all.
- **Scanning a `List` with `contains` for uniqueness.** That is O(n) per check; a `Set` does it in O(1) and rejects duplicates automatically.
- **Using `LinkedList` as a default list.** `ArrayList` wins for almost everything; `LinkedList.get(i)` inside a loop is O(n^2).
- **Forgetting thread safety.** A shared `HashMap` under concurrent writes can corrupt; use `ConcurrentHashMap` when multiple threads touch it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- First question: **lookup by key?** -> Map.
- Next: **duplicates allowed?** Yes -> List; No -> Set.
- Pick variant by **ordering**: Hash (none), Linked (insertion), Tree (sorted).
- Pick by **access pattern**: `ArrayList` (random), `ArrayDeque` (queue/stack).
- Final branch: **thread safety** -> `ConcurrentHashMap`, `CopyOnWriteArrayList`.
- Default to `ArrayList` and `HashMap` when no special need applies.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: I treat it as a short decision tree rather than memorizing defaults. The first question is about the shape of the data: am I looking things up by a key? If the access pattern is given an id, fetch the object, then I need a Map, because that turns lookups into constant time instead of scanning a list. If I'm not looking up by key, the next question is whether duplicates are allowed. If duplicates are fine and order matters, I want a List — ArrayList by default, or ArrayDeque if it's really a queue or a stack. If elements must be unique, I want a Set. Once the family is decided, I choose the variant by ordering needs. The Hash variant is fastest and has no order, the Linked variant preserves insertion order, and the Tree variant keeps things sorted and supports range queries, at log-n cost. So for a Map I'd pick HashMap, LinkedHashMap, or TreeMap, and for a Set, HashSet, LinkedHashSet, or TreeSet, using the same logic. The last branch I always check is thread safety. If the structure is shared across threads, I don't use the plain version — I reach for ConcurrentHashMap, or CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-heavy lists. When none of these special needs apply, the safe defaults are ArrayList and HashMap. Walking through the questions out loud — key lookup, duplicates, ordering, access pattern, concurrency — shows the interviewer I have a real process, not just a memorized answer.

questions.question: What useful methods does the Collections utility class provide?
questions.title: Collections Utility Class
questions.direct_answer: **Collections** is a `java.util` utility class of **static helpers**: `sort`, `reverse`, `shuffle`, `binarySearch`, `max`/`min`, `frequency`, `unmodifiableList`/`unmodifiableMap` (read-only views), `synchronizedList` (thread-safe wrapper), and `emptyList`/`singletonList`. In modern Java, prefer `List.of(...)` for true immutable lists over `unmodifiableList`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Familiarity with the standard library so you don't reinvent sort/min/max manually
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Collections (class) with Collection (interface), or thinking unmodifiableList copies the data
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note unmodifiableList is a read-only VIEW (backing list changes still show), while List.of is a true immutable copy

sections.title: The Standard-Library Toolbox
sections.content:
**`Collections`** (plural) is a final utility class — like `Math` — holding only **static methods** that operate on collections. You never create an instance; you just call the helpers.

It saves you from hand-writing common operations: `sort` and `reverse` for ordering, `shuffle` for randomization, `binarySearch` on a sorted list, `max`/`min` for extremes, `frequency` to count occurrences, and `swap`/`fill`/`nCopies` for bulk edits.

It also provides **wrappers**: `unmodifiableList`/`unmodifiableMap` return a **read-only view** (mutating throws `UnsupportedOperationException`), and `synchronizedList`/`synchronizedMap` add coarse thread safety.

A key subtlety: `unmodifiableList` wraps the original list, so changes to the backing list still appear through the view. For a truly immutable snapshot use `List.of(...)`.

> **Remember the names:** `Collections` (plural) is the toolbox; `Collection` (singular) is the interface.

sections.title: Collections Methods by Category
sections.content:
blue|Ordering|~Rearrange elements|sort, reverse|shuffle|swap, rotate
emerald|Search & stats|~Query a collection|binarySearch (sorted)|max, min|frequency, disjoint
amber|Read-only views|~Prevent mutation|unmodifiableList / Map / Set|throws on modify|use List.of for true immutability
rose|Thread safety|~Coarse locking|synchronizedList / Map|wraps every method|prefer concurrent collections

sections.title: Picking a Collections Helper
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD C["Collections utility class"] --> O["Ordering
sort, reverse, shuffle"] C --> SE["Search and stats
binarySearch, max, min, frequency"] C --> V["Read-only views
unmodifiableList / Map / Set"] C --> T["Thread safety
synchronizedList / Map"] V --> IM["For true immutability
use List.of or List.copyOf"] ```

sections.title: Common Collections Helpers
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Collections vs Collection.** `Collections` is the utility class; `Collection` is the interface — don't use `Collections` as a type.
- **Thinking `unmodifiableList` copies.** It's a *view* over the original; mutate the backing list and the view changes too. Use `List.of` / `List.copyOf` for an immutable copy.
- **Reinventing the wheel.** Writing manual loops for sort/max/min instead of calling the helpers.
- **Relying on `synchronizedList` for compound actions.** Iteration still needs external synchronization; prefer concurrent collections.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `Collections` = static helpers; `Collection` = the interface.
- Ordering: `sort`, `reverse`, `shuffle`, `swap`, `rotate`.
- Search/stats: `binarySearch` (sorted only), `max`, `min`, `frequency`.
- `unmodifiableList` = **read-only view**, not a copy; throws on mutation.
- `List.of` / `List.copyOf` = **true immutable** lists (preferred).
- `synchronizedList` adds coarse thread safety; concurrent collections are usually better.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Collections, with an s, is a utility class full of static helper methods that operate on collections, similar to how the Math class works. The ones I reach for most are about ordering: sort to order a list, reverse to flip it, and shuffle to randomize it. There are search and statistics helpers too — binarySearch on a sorted list, max and min to find extremes, and frequency to count how many times an element appears. It also has bulk helpers like swap, fill, and nCopies. Two categories are especially worth knowing for interviews. First, the read-only wrappers: unmodifiableList, unmodifiableMap, and unmodifiableSet return a view that throws an UnsupportedOperationException if you try to modify it. The subtle catch is that it's a view over the original list, not a copy — so if the backing list changes, those changes show through the view. If you want a genuinely immutable snapshot, the modern approach is List.of or List.copyOf, which create a true immutable list. Second, the thread-safety wrappers: synchronizedList and synchronizedMap wrap every method in a lock, but they're coarse and iteration still needs external synchronization, so for real concurrency I'd prefer ConcurrentHashMap or CopyOnWriteArrayList. The big mistakes to avoid are confusing Collections the class with Collection the interface, assuming unmodifiableList makes a copy when it's really a view, and writing manual loops to sort or find a maximum when these helpers already exist.

questions.question: What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator in Java?
questions.title: Comparable vs Comparator
questions.direct_answer: **Comparable** defines a type's **natural ordering** via `compareTo(T)` implemented inside the class itself (one ordering). **Comparator** is an **external** ordering strategy via `compare(T, T)`, defined outside the class, so you can have many orderings and sort types you don't own. Use Comparable for the default sort, Comparator for custom or multiple sorts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know which interface lives inside vs outside the class and when to use each
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing up compareTo (one arg) with compare (two args), or thinking you can only sort with Comparable

sections.title: Natural Order vs External Strategy
sections.content:
**`Comparable`** is implemented *inside* the class to define its **natural ordering** — `String` sorts alphabetically, `Integer` numerically. Its method is `int compareTo(T other)`: return negative if `this` is less, zero if equal, positive if greater. A type has exactly **one** natural order.

**`Comparator`** is a separate object that defines an ordering *externally* via `int compare(T a, T b)`. Because it's external, you can define **many** comparators — by name, by age, by date — and you can sort types whose source you don't control.

The **rule of thumb**: if there's one obvious default ordering and you own the class, make it `Comparable`. For everything else — custom rules, multiple sorts, third-party types — pass a `Comparator`.

Modern factory methods make comparators concise: `comparing`, `comparingInt`, `thenComparing`, `reversed`, and `nullsFirst`.

> **The gotcha:** `compareTo` takes **one** argument; `compare` takes **two** — mixing them up will not compile.

sections.title: Comparable vs Comparator
sections.content:
| Aspect | Comparable | Comparator |
|---|---|---|
| Package | `java.lang` | `java.util` |
| Method | `compareTo(T o)` (1 arg) | `compare(T a, T b)` (2 args) |
| Location | Inside the class | Separate object / lambda |
| Orderings | One (natural) | Many |
| Sort call | `Collections.sort(list)` | `list.sort(cmp)` |
| Own the class? | Must (to implement it) | Not required |

sections.title: Inside vs Outside the Class
sections.content:
blue|Comparable|~Natural order|implemented in the class|compareTo, one argument|one ordering per type
emerald|Comparator|~External strategy|separate object or lambda|compare, two arguments|many orderings possible
amber|When to use which|~Rule of thumb|one obvious default -> Comparable|custom or multiple -> Comparator|works on types you don't own
rose|Return value|~Same convention|negative = less|zero = equal|positive = greater

sections.title: Comparable or Comparator?
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD Q["Need to sort a type?"] --> A{"Own the class and
one obvious order?"} A -- yes --> B["Implement Comparable
compareTo, natural order"] A -- no --> C["Pass a Comparator
compare, external strategy"] C --> D["Chain it
comparing, thenComparing, reversed"] ```

sections.title: Only a natural order — can't sort by other fields
Comparator: many orderings, chained and reusable
When to Use Each
sections.content:
Use **Comparable** when the type has one obvious default ordering you own — IDs, timestamps, names — so `Collections.sort(list)` and `TreeSet`/`TreeMap` just work.

Use **Comparator** when you need **multiple** orderings, a **custom** rule, descending order, or to sort a **type you don't control**. Modern factory methods (`comparing`, `comparingInt`, `thenComparing`, `reversed`, `nullsFirst`) make comparators concise and chainable.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Swapping the method signatures.** `compareTo` takes **one** argument (the other object); `compare` takes **two**. Mixing them up will not compile.
- **Thinking you can only sort with `Comparable`.** `Comparator` is the more flexible tool — many orderings, and it works on types you do not own.
- **Returning booleans instead of negative/zero/positive.** Both methods return an `int`: negative, zero, or positive — not `true`/`false`.
- **Forgetting `TreeSet`/`TreeMap` need an ordering.** They use natural order via `Comparable`, or a supplied `Comparator`; without either you get a `ClassCastException` at runtime.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Comparable** (`java.lang`) — `compareTo(T)`, natural order, one per type, inside the class.
- **Comparator** (`java.util`) — `compare(T, T)`, external, many orderings, any type.
- `compareTo` takes **one** argument; `compare` takes **two**.
- `TreeSet`/`TreeMap` use natural order, or a supplied `Comparator`.
- Chain comparators: `comparing(...).thenComparing(...).reversed()`.
- Return value: negative / zero / positive for less / equal / greater.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Comparable and Comparator both define ordering, but they live in different places and serve different needs. Comparable is implemented inside the class itself and defines the type's natural ordering. Its method is compareTo, which takes a single argument — the other object — and returns a negative number if this object is smaller, zero if they're equal, or a positive number if it's larger. String sorts alphabetically and Integer sorts numerically because they implement Comparable. The key limitation is that a type has exactly one natural order. Comparator is different: it's a separate object that defines ordering externally. Its method is compare, which takes two arguments and compares them. Because it lives outside the class, you can create as many comparators as you like — sort employees by name, by age, by salary — and you can even sort classes whose source code you don't own, which you can't do with Comparable. So the rule of thumb is: if there's one obvious default ordering and you own the class, make it Comparable. For anything situational — custom rules, multiple sort orders, descending order, or third-party types — pass a Comparator. A nice modern detail to mention is comparator chaining. You can write Comparator.comparing by one field, then thenComparing for a tiebreaker, and reversed to flip the direction, all in one readable expression. The classic mistakes are mixing up the method signatures — compareTo takes one argument, compare takes two — and thinking you can only sort with Comparable, when Comparator is actually the more flexible tool.
